claims.text: The starting material consists of crystalline, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles containing five or more metals.
Carbothermal shock synthesis is the proposed single intervention.
Carbothermal shock synthesis can overcome structural or chemical instability during catalytic operation at 773–1173 K.
Carbothermal shock synthesis can rapidly fabricate high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Carbothermal shock synthesis induces a high-entropy effect.
The high-entropy effect leads to formation of a single random solid-solution phase.
The single random solid-solution phase causes severe lattice distortion.
The single random solid-solution phase causes sluggish diffusion kinetics.
The single random solid-solution phase produces a cocktail effect.
The high-entropy effect, lattice distortion, sluggish diffusion, and cocktail effect preserve nanoparticle stability.
Carbothermal-shock-synthesized nanoparticles will have improved structural and chemical stability relative to nanoparticles made without the intervention.
The predicted stability improvement applies throughout 773–1173 K.
The relevant time boundary is seconds to minutes.
The compositional boundary is five or more metals.
The exact stability-preserving mechanisms are not fully understood.
The proposed experiment compares carbothermal-shock-synthesized nanoparticles with nanoparticles made without carbothermal shock synthesis.
The experiment will measure structural stability, chemical stability, and catalytic activity.
The hypothesis is considered falsified if the treated nanoparticles show no improvement in stability or catalytic activity relative to the control.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome only requires improved structural or chemical stability, but the falsification rule also treats lack of catalytic-activity improvement as sufficient for falsification. Thus, a sample could satisfy the stated stability prediction yet be declared falsified because its activity is unchanged.
